text: Number of moles and number of molecules in 1.4187 L of $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ at STP respectively are
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
At STP, according to Avogadro’s law, $1$ mole of any gas occupies $22.4\text{L}$.

So, number of moles of $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ is

$n=\frac{V}{22.4}=\frac{1.4187}{22.4}$

$n=0.0633\text{mol}$

Now, number of molecules

$=n\times N_{A}$

where $N_{A}=6.022\times 10^{23}$

So,

$\text{Number of molecules}=0.0633\times 6.022\times 10^{23}$

$=3.812\times 10^{22}$

Hence, the correct answer is:

$0.0633\text{mol ;}3.812\times 10^{22}\text{molecules}$

So, Option B is correct.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift

text: What is the ratio of wave number of first line (lowest energy line) of Balmer series of H atomic spectrum to first line of its Brackett series?
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For hydrogen spectrum, the wave number is given by the Rydberg formula:

$\bar{ν}=R\left (\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}\right )$

where:

$n_{1}$ = lower energy level

$n_{2}$ = higher energy level

$n_{2}>n_{1}$

Now let us find the first line of each series.

1. First line of Balmer series
For Balmer series:

$n_{1}=2$

The first line means transition from $n_{2}=3$ to $n_{1}=2$.

So,

$\bar{ν}_{B}=R\left (\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{3^{2}}\right )=R\left (\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}\right )$

$\bar{ν}_{B}=R\left (\frac{9-4}{36}\right )=\frac{5R}{36}$

2. First line of Brackett series
For Brackett series:

$n_{1}=4$

The first line means transition from $n_{2}=5$ to $n_{1}=4$.

So,

$\bar{ν}_{Br}=R\left (\frac{1}{4^{2}}-\frac{1}{5^{2}}\right )=R\left (\frac{1}{16}-\frac{1}{25}\right )$

$\bar{ν}_{Br}=R\left (\frac{25-16}{400}\right )=\frac{9R}{400}$

3. Required ratio
$\bar{ν}_{B}:\bar{ν}_{Br}=\frac{5R}{36}:\frac{9R}{400}$

Cancel $R$:

$=\frac{5}{36}:\frac{9}{400}$

$=\frac{5}{36}\times \frac{400}{9}$

So ratio:

$\bar{ν}_{B}:\bar{ν}_{Br}=\frac{2000}{324}=\frac{500}{81}$

Now,

$\frac{500}{81}=\frac{5\times 100}{81}$

and

$\frac{100}{81}\approx 1.23$

So,

$\bar{ν}_{B}:\bar{ν}_{Br}=5:0.81$

Therefore, the correct answer is:

$\text{Option B}5:0.81$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift

text: Which of the following is correct set of 4 quantum numbers of $19^{\text{th}}$ electron in Chromium (Atomic number $=24$ ) in accordance with Aufbau principle?
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Using the Aufbau principle, we fill electrons in the order:

$1s,2s,2p,3s,3p,4s,3d,\ldots$

Now let us count electrons one by one up to the $19^{\text{th}}$ electron.

$1s^{2}\Rightarrow 2$ electrons

$2s^{2}\Rightarrow 4$ electrons

$2p^{6}\Rightarrow 10$ electrons

$3s^{2}\Rightarrow 12$ electrons

$3p^{6}\Rightarrow 18$ electrons

So, the $19^{\text{th}}$ electron enters the $4s$ orbital.

For a $4s$ electron:

$n=4$

for $s$-orbital, $l=0$

when $l=0$, only possible value of $m$ is $0$

for the first electron in this orbital, $s=+\dfrac{1}{2}$

Thus, the set of four quantum numbers is:

$n=4,l=0,m=0,s=+\frac{1}{2}$

So, the correct option is:

$\text{Option D}$

Note: Chromium actually has exceptional configuration $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$, but the question clearly says "in accordance with Aufbau principle", so we must place the $19^{\text{th}}$ electron in $4s$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift

text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : For an ideal gas, heat capacity at constant volume is always greater than the heat capacity at constant pressure.

Statement II : In a constant volume process, no work is produced and all the heat withdrawn goes into the chaotic motion and is reflected by a temperature increase of the ideal gas.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For an ideal gas, we know that

$C_{p}-C_{v}=R$

where $R>0$.

So,

$C_{p}>C_{v}$

This means Statement I is false, because it says that heat capacity at constant volume is greater than heat capacity at constant pressure.

Now look at Statement II.

In a constant volume process,

$\Delta V=0$

So the work done is

$W=P\Delta V=0$

From the first law of thermodynamics,

$Q=\Delta U+W$

Since $W=0$,

$Q=\Delta U$

For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature. Therefore, the heat supplied or withdrawn at constant volume changes the internal energy, which is associated with the random or chaotic motion of molecules, and this is reflected in a change in temperature.

So Statement II is true in the NCERT sense.

Hence, the correct answer is:

$\text{Option D}$

That is, Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift

text:
At $\mathrm{T}(\mathrm{K})$, the equilibrium constant of 

$\mathrm{A}_{2}(g)+\mathrm{B}_{2}(g)⇌\mathrm{C}(g)$ is $2.7\times 10^{-5}$. 

What is the equilibrium constant for 

$\frac{1}{3}\mathrm{A}_{2}(\mathrm{g})+\frac{1}{3}\mathrm{B}_{2}(\mathrm{g})⇌\frac{1}{3}\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{g})$ at the same temperature?
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For the reaction

$\mathrm{A}_{2}(\mathrm{g})+\mathrm{B}_{2}(\mathrm{g})⇌\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{g})$

the equilibrium constant is given as

$K=2.7\times 10^{-5}$

Now the new reaction is

$\frac{1}{3}\mathrm{A}_{2}(\mathrm{g})+\frac{1}{3}\mathrm{B}_{2}(\mathrm{g})⇌\frac{1}{3}\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{g})$

This reaction is obtained by dividing all the coefficients of the original reaction by $3$.

According to the rule for equilibrium constants:

if the coefficients of a balanced chemical equation are multiplied by $n$, then the new equilibrium constant becomes $K^{n}$

if the coefficients are divided by $n$, then the new equilibrium constant becomes $K^{1/n}$

So here,

$K^{'}=K^{1/3}$

Therefore,

$K^{'}=\left (2.7\times 10^{-5}\right )^{1/3}$

Now calculate:

$2.7=(0.3)^{3}\times 100$

But it is easier to check directly:

$(3\times 10^{-2})^{3}=27\times 10^{-6}=2.7\times 10^{-5}$

So,

$\left (2.7\times 10^{-5}\right )^{1/3}=3\times 10^{-2}$

Hence, the correct answer is:

$3\times 10^{-2}$

So, Option D is correct.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift

text: In order to oxidise a mixture of 1 mole each of $\mathrm{FeC}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4},\mathrm{Fe}_{2}(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4})_{3},\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$ and $\mathrm{Fe}_{2}(\mathrm{SO}_{4})_{3}$ in acidic medium, the number of moles of $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ required is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In acidic medium, $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ acts as a strong oxidising agent.

So, we need to find which species in the given mixture can be oxidised further.

The mixture contains $1$ mole each of:

$\mathrm{FeC}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4}$

$\mathrm{Fe}_{2}(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4})_{3}$

$\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$

$\mathrm{Fe}_{2}(\mathrm{SO}_{4})_{3}$

Now let us examine each compound.

1. $\mathrm{FeC}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4}$
This is ferrous oxalate, so it contains:

$\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ : can be oxidised to $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$

$\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-}$ : can be oxidised to $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$

Oxidation of $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$
$\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\to \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+\mathrm{e}^{-}$

So, $1$ mole of $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ gives $1$ mole electron.

Oxidation of oxalate
$\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-}\to 2\mathrm{CO}_{2}+2\mathrm{e}^{-}$

So, $1$ mole of $\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-}$ gives $2$ moles electrons.

Hence, $1$ mole of $\mathrm{FeC}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4}$ gives total electrons:

$1+2=3$

2. $\mathrm{Fe}_{2}(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4})_{3}$
This contains:

$\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ : already in higher oxidation state, so no oxidation

$3$ oxalate ions: each can be oxidised

Each oxalate ion gives $2$ electrons, so $3$ oxalates give:

$3\times 2=6$

Thus, $1$ mole of $\mathrm{Fe}_{2}(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4})_{3}$ gives $6$ electrons.

3. $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$
This contains:

$\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ : can be oxidised to $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$

$\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ : sulphur is already at maximum oxidation state $+6$, so no oxidation

Thus, $1$ mole of $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$ gives:

$1\text{electron}$

4. $\mathrm{Fe}_{2}(\mathrm{SO}_{4})_{3}$
This contains:

$\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ : cannot be oxidised further here

$\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ : cannot be oxidised further

So, electrons given:

$0$

Total electrons released
$3+6+1+0=10$

Electrons accepted by $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ in acidic medium
In acidic medium:

$\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+8\mathrm{H}^{+}+5\mathrm{e}^{-}\to \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+4\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$

So, $1$ mole of $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ accepts $5$ moles of electrons.

Therefore, moles of $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ required:

$\frac{10}{5}=2$

Final answer
$2$

So, the correct option is Option B.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift

text:
Consider the first order reaction $\mathrm{R}\to \mathrm{P}$.

The fraction of molecules decomposed in the given first order reaction can be expressed as
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For a first order reaction

$\mathrm{R}\to \mathrm{P}$

the integrated rate law is

$[R]_{t}=[R]_{0}e^{-k_{1}t}$

where:

$[R]_{0}$ = initial concentration of reactant

$[R]_{t}$ = concentration after time $t$

Now, the fraction of molecules left undecomposed after time $t$ is

$\frac{[R]_{t}}{[R]_{0}}=e^{-k_{1}t}$

So, the fraction of molecules decomposed is

$1-\frac{[R]_{t}}{[R]_{0}}=1-e^{-k_{1}t}$

Hence, the correct answer is

$1-e^{-k_{1}t}$

So, Option D is correct.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift

text: A monoatomic anion $(\mathrm{A}^{-})$ has 45 neutrons and 36 electrons. Atomic mass, group in the periodic table and physical state at room temperature of the element (A) respectively are
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For a monoatomic anion $A^{-}$:

Number of electrons in $A^{-}$ $=36$

Since it is an anion with charge $-1$, the neutral atom $A$ must have one electron less.

So, number of electrons in neutral atom $A$:

$36-1=35$

Hence, atomic number of $A$ is $35$.

This element is bromine.

Now, number of neutrons $=45$

So, mass number:

$\text{Mass number}=\text{protons}+\text{neutrons}=35+45=80$

Thus, atomic mass number is:

$80$

Now let us find the group.

Bromine $(Z=35)$ belongs to group 17 in the periodic table.

Also, bromine is a liquid at room temperature.

So, the correct answer is:

$\text{Option A:}80,17,\text{liquid}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift

text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : The covalency of oxygen is generally two but it can exceed upto four. The oxidation state of oxygen in $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ is -2 and in $\mathrm{OF}_{2}$ it is +2 .

Statement II : The anomalous behaviour of oxygen when compared to the other elements of group 16 is due to its small size and high electronegativity.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Analysis of Statement I:

Covalency of Oxygen: The electronic configuration of oxygen is $1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{4}$. In its outermost shell ($n=2$), it possesses exactly four orbitals available for bonding: one $2s$ orbital and three $2p$ orbitals. Because oxygen is a Period 2 element, it completely lacks empty $d$-orbitals. Consequently, its maximum covalency is restricted to a maximum of 4. While oxygen generally shows a normal covalency of 2 (as seen in $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$), it can exceed this completely up to 4 in certain scenarios (co-ordinating to maximum four atoms as seen theoretically, and a covalency of 3 is commonly observed in the hydronium ion, $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$). So, the first part of the statement is correct.

Oxidation States:

In $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$, oxygen is more electronegative than sulphur. Here, sulphur has an oxidation state of +4, and each oxygen atom securely takes an oxidation state of -2.

In $\mathrm{OF}_{2}$, fluorine is the most electronegative element in the periodic table. Because fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, each fluorine atom takes an oxidation state of -1. To maintain neutrality in the $\mathrm{OF}_{2}$ molecule, the oxidation state of oxygen must be +2. 

Therefore, the second part of the statement is perfectly correct as well. 

Conclusion: Statement I is true.

Analysis of Statement II:

In the $p$-block elements, the first member of every group always differs significantly from the heavier members of the same group. According to the NCERT, the anomalous behavior of oxygen compared to the rest of the group 16 elements (like Sulphur, Selenium, etc.) is prominently due to:

Its exceptionally small atomic size.

Its high electronegativity.

The non-availability of $d$-orbitals in its valence shell.

Because of its small size and high electronegativity, it readily forms strong $pπ-pπ$ double bonds and extensive hydrogen bonds, uniquely distinguishing it from other group elements. The statement accurately lists the main reasons, so it is correct.

Conclusion: Statement II is true.

Final Conclusion:

Since both the provided statements are factually correct based on standard chemical principles, we determine the correct option.

Correct Answer:

Option A

Both Statement I and Statement II are true

text:
The correct statements among the following are,

A. $\mathrm{Mo}(\mathrm{VI})$ and $\mathrm{W}(\mathrm{VI})$ are less stable than $\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{VI})$.

B. $\mathrm{Ce}^{4+}$ and $\mathrm{Tb}^{4+}$ are oxidant while $\mathrm{Eu}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Yb}^{2+}$ are reductant.

C. Cm and Am have seven unpaired electrons.

D. Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Statement A
$\mathrm{Mo}(\mathrm{VI})$ and $\mathrm{W}(\mathrm{VI})$ are less stable than $\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{VI})$.

This statement is incorrect.

In group 6 elements:

$\mathrm{Cr}$, $\mathrm{Mo}$ and $\mathrm{W}$ commonly show the $+6$ oxidation state.

The higher oxidation states become more stable for heavier members of the group.

So,

$\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{VI})$ is strongly oxidising and less stable comparatively,

while $\mathrm{Mo}(\mathrm{VI})$ and especially $\mathrm{W}(\mathrm{VI})$ are more stable.

Hence, A is false.

Statement B
$\mathrm{Ce}^{4+}$ and $\mathrm{Tb}^{4+}$ are oxidant while $\mathrm{Eu}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Yb}^{2+}$ are reductant.

This statement is correct.

Reason:

$\mathrm{Ce}^{4+}$ tends to change to $\mathrm{Ce}^{3+}$, so it acts as an oxidising agent.

$\mathrm{Tb}^{4+}$ also tends to reduce to $\mathrm{Tb}^{3+}$, so it is an oxidant.

$\mathrm{Eu}^{2+}$ tends to change to $\mathrm{Eu}^{3+}$, so it donates electrons and acts as a reducing agent.

$\mathrm{Yb}^{2+}$ similarly tends to go to $\mathrm{Yb}^{3+}$, so it is also a reductant.

Hence, B is true.

Statement C
Cm and Am have seven unpaired electrons.

This statement is incorrect.

Let us see the electronic configurations:

$\mathrm{Am}$ : $[Rn]\qquad 5f^{7}7s^{2}$

$\mathrm{Cm}$ : $[Rn]\qquad 5f^{7}6d^{1}7s^{2}$

Now count unpaired electrons:

In $\mathrm{Am}$, $5f^{7}$ gives 7 unpaired electrons

In $\mathrm{Cm}$, $5f^{7}$ gives 7 unpaired, and $6d^{1}$ gives 1 more unpaired

So $\mathrm{Cm}$ has 8 unpaired electrons, not 7.

Hence, C is false.

Statement D
Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction.

This statement is correct.

Reason:

In actinoids, the $5f$ electrons shield the nuclear charge even more poorly than the $4f$ electrons do in lanthanoids.

Therefore, the decrease in atomic and ionic size across actinoids is greater.

Hence, D is true.

Final conclusion
Correct statements are:

$B\text{and}D\text{only}$

So the correct option is:

$\text{Option C}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift

Match the LIST-I with LIST-II

  

    List-I
Complex ion

    List-II
Calculated spin only magnetic moment (BM)

  

  

    A.

    $[\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})_{6}]^{2+}$

    I.

    3.87

  

  

    B.

    $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})_{6}]^{2+}$

    II.

    5.92

  

  

    C.

    $[\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})_{6}]^{2+}$

    III.

    4.90

  

  

    D.

    $[\mathrm{Mn}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})_{6}]^{2+}$

    IV.

    1.73

  

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For matching, we use the spin-only magnetic moment formula:

$μ=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{BM}$

where $n$ = number of unpaired electrons.

Since $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ is a weak field ligand, all these octahedral complexes will be high spin.

Now find oxidation state, electronic configuration, number of unpaired electrons, and then magnetic moment.

A. $[\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})_{6}]^{2+}$
Here, chromium is in $+2$ oxidation state.

Atomic number of Cr = $24$

Neutral Cr:

$\mathrm{Cr}=[\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{1}$

So,

$\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}=3d^{4}$

For high spin $d^{4}$, number of unpaired electrons:

$n=4$

Thus,

$μ=\sqrt{4(4+2)}=\sqrt{24}\approx 4.90\text{BM}$

So, A $\to$ III

B. $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})_{6}]^{2+}$
Cobalt is in $+2$ oxidation state.

Atomic number of Co = $27$

$\mathrm{Co}^{2+}=3d^{7}$

For high spin $d^{7}$, number of unpaired electrons:

$n=3$

Thus,

$μ=\sqrt{3(3+2)}=\sqrt{15}\approx 3.87\text{BM}$

So, B $\to$ I

C. $[\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})_{6}]^{2+}$
Copper is in $+2$ oxidation state.

Atomic number of Cu = $29$

$\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}=3d^{9}$

For $d^{9}$, number of unpaired electrons:

$n=1$

Thus,

$μ=\sqrt{1(1+2)}=\sqrt{3}\approx 1.73\text{BM}$

So, C $\to$ IV

D. $[\mathrm{Mn}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})_{6}]^{2+}$
Manganese is in $+2$ oxidation state.

Atomic number of Mn = $25$

$\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}=3d^{5}$

For high spin $d^{5}$, number of unpaired electrons:

$n=5$

Thus,

$μ=\sqrt{5(5+2)}=\sqrt{35}\approx 5.92\text{BM}$

So, D $\to$ II

Final matching
$\text{A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II}$

So the correct option is:

$\text{Option D}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift

text:
Increasing order of electron withdrawing power of following functional groups is :

a. -CN

b. -COOH

c. $-\mathrm{NO}_{2}$

d. $-\mathrm{I}$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To understand this question, we need to look at the Inductive effect, specifically the negative inductive effect ($-I$ effect), which determines the electron-withdrawing power of a functional group. 

According to the principles of organic chemistry laid out in your NCERT textbook, the electron-withdrawing nature of a group depends on the electronegativity of the atoms present in the group and their arrangement.

The standard decreasing order of the $-I$ effect (electron-withdrawing power) for various functional groups is:

$-\mathrm{NO}_{2}>-\mathrm{CN}>-\mathrm{COOH}>-\mathrm{F}>-\mathrm{Cl}>-\mathrm{Br}>-\mathrm{I}>-\mathrm{OH}>-\mathrm{OCH}_{3}>-\mathrm{C}_{6}\mathrm{H}_{5}>-\mathrm{H}$

Let us analyze the functional groups given in the question:

$-\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ (c): This group has a nitrogen atom bonded to two highly electronegative oxygen atoms, and the nitrogen carries a formal positive charge. This makes it a very strong electron-withdrawing group.

$-\mathrm{CN}$ (a): The carbon in the cyanide group is $sp$ hybridized, which makes it more electronegative. Coupled with the electronegative nitrogen atom, it exerts a strong $-I$ effect, but it is slightly weaker than $-\mathrm{NO}_{2}$.

$-\mathrm{COOH}$ (b): This group contains a carbonyl carbon attached to a hydroxyl oxygen. It shows a moderate $-I$ effect, which is weaker than both $-\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ and $-\mathrm{CN}$.

$-\mathrm{I}$ (d): Iodine is a halogen. While halogens are electronegative, iodine has the largest atomic size and the lowest electronegativity among the common halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine). Hence, it has the weakest $-I$ effect out of the groups listed here.

Based on this analysis, the decreasing order of their electron-withdrawing power is:

$\mathrm{c}(-\mathrm{NO}_{2})>\mathrm{a}(-\mathrm{CN})>\mathrm{b}(-\mathrm{COOH})>\mathrm{d}(-\mathrm{I})$

Therefore, rearranging them into the increasing order gives:

$\mathrm{d}<\mathrm{b}<\mathrm{a}<\mathrm{c}$

This perfectly matches Option C.

Correct Answer:

Option C

$\mathrm{d}<\mathrm{b}<\mathrm{a}<\mathrm{c}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift

The products, $2~\mathrm{HCHO}$, $\mathrm{OHC}-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{CHO}$ and $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{COCH}{}_{3}$, contain 10 C atoms and 8 C=O groups, so X has 10 C atoms and four C=C bonds, each cleaved into two C=O.

The two $\mathrm{HCHO}$ come from two $=\mathrm{CH}_{2}$ groups. The middle carbon of each tricarbonyl product carried one of these $=\mathrm{CH}_{2}$ groups, so in X one such carbon was flanked by two $=\mathrm{CH}-$ carbons and the other by two $=\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{CH}_{3})-$ carbons.

X is a hydrocarbon, so every remaining carbonyl end came from a C=C: each $\mathrm{CHO}$ carbon was double-bonded to a $\mathrm{COCH}{}_{3}$ carbon. These two $\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{CH}_{3})$ bonds join the two fragments into a six-membered ring:


[IMG]

This is structure (D). Structure (C) carries three $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$ groups (11 C), and (A) and (B) have only one ring C=C, so their rings cannot split into two fragments.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

text:
$\text{Match the LIST-I with LIST-II}$

  

    $\begin{array}{l} \text{List-I} \\ \text{Name of reaction} \end{array}$

    $\begin{array}{l} \text{List-II} \\ \text{Reagent or catalyst used} \end{array}$

  

  

    A.

    Finkelstein reaction

    I.

    $\mathrm{SbF}_{3}$

  

  

    B.

    Swarts reaction

    II.

    Na, dry ether

  

  

    C.

    Sandmeyer's reaction

    III.

    NaI

  

  

    D.

    Fittig reaction

    IV.

    $\mathrm{Cu}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$

  

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
A. Finkelstein reaction:

This is a halogen exchange reaction used specifically for the preparation of alkyl iodides. In this reaction, alkyl chlorides or bromides are treated with sodium iodide ($\mathrm{NaI}$) in dry acetone. 

Therefore, A matches with III.

B. Swarts reaction:

This reaction is the preferred method for the synthesis of alkyl fluorides. It involves heating an alkyl chloride or bromide in the presence of a metallic fluoride. Some of the common fluorinating agents used are $\mathrm{AgF}$, $\mathrm{Hg}_{2}\mathrm{F}_{2}$, $\mathrm{CoF}_{2}$, or antimony trifluoride ($\mathrm{SbF}_{3}$).

Therefore, B matches with I.

C. Sandmeyer's reaction:

This reaction is used to prepare haloarenes (like chlorobenzene or bromobenzene) from benzene diazonium chloride. The diazonium salt is treated with a cuprous halide, such as cuprous chloride ($\mathrm{Cu}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$ or $\mathrm{CuCl}$), to replace the diazonium group with a halogen. 

Therefore, C matches with IV.

D. Fittig reaction:

This reaction involves aryl halides. When an aryl halide is treated with sodium ($\mathrm{Na}$) in the presence of dry ether, two aryl groups join together to form a diaryl compound (like biphenyl). 

Therefore, D matches with II.

Summary of Matches:

A (Finkelstein reaction) $\to$ III ($\mathrm{NaI}$)

B (Swarts reaction) $\to$ I ($\mathrm{SbF}_{3}$)

C (Sandmeyer's reaction) $\to$ IV ($\mathrm{Cu}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$)

D (Fittig reaction) $\to$ II ($\mathrm{Na}$, dry ether)

Comparing our findings with the given options, the correct combination is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

Option B is the correct answer.

text: According to Lewis theory, the total number of $σ$ bond-pairs and lone pair of electrons around the central atom of $\mathrm{XeO}_{6}{}^{4-}$ ion is $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In $\mathrm{XeO}{}_{6}{}^{4-}$, Xe (8 valence electrons) is the central atom bonded to six O atoms; the ion has $8+6\times 6+4=48$ valence electrons.

In the Lewis structure Xe forms two $\mathrm{Xe}=\mathrm{O}$ bonds and four Xe–O single bonds to $\mathrm{O}{}^{-}$ atoms, which uses all $2\times 2+4\times 1=8$ valence electrons of Xe, so no lone pair remains on Xe.


[IMG]

Each Xe–O link, single or double, contains exactly one $σ$ bond, so Xe carries 6 $σ$ bond pairs and 0 lone pairs.

$\text{Total}=6+0=6$

Hence, the answer is 6.

text:
2.0 g of a bromo hydrocarbon $(\mathrm{X})$ was subjected to Carius analysis, gave 3.36 g of AgBr . The percentage of carbon in the compound $(\mathrm{X})$ is $26.7%$. Total number of carbon atoms in the empirical formula for compound $(\mathrm{X})$ is $____$ .

(Given molar mass in $\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}\mathrm{H}:1,\mathrm{C}:12,\mathrm{Br}:80,\mathrm{Ag}:108$ )
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In Carius analysis, all bromine is converted into $\mathrm{AgBr}$.

Given:

Mass of $\mathrm{AgBr}=3.36\mathrm{g}$

Molar mass of $\mathrm{AgBr}$:

$108+80=188$

So, mass of bromine in $3.36\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{AgBr}$ is

$\text{Mass of Br}=\frac{80}{188}\times 3.36$

$=\frac{268.8}{188}=1.43\mathrm{g}\text{(approximately)}$

Mass of compound taken $=2.0\mathrm{g}$

So, percentage of bromine is

$%\mathrm{Br}=\frac{1.43}{2.0}\times 100=71.5%$

Given:

$%\mathrm{C}=26.7%$

Since it is a hydrocarbon containing only C, H and Br,

$%\mathrm{H}=100-26.7-71.5=1.8%$

Take $100\mathrm{g}$ of compound.

Then:

Carbon $=26.7\mathrm{g}$

Hydrogen $=1.8\mathrm{g}$

Bromine $=71.5\mathrm{g}$

Now moles:

$\text{Moles of C}=\frac{26.7}{12}=2.225$

$\text{Moles of H}=\frac{1.8}{1}=1.8$

$\text{Moles of Br}=\frac{71.5}{80}=0.894$

$\mathrm{C}:\mathrm{H}:\mathrm{Br}=\frac{2.225}{0.894}:\frac{1.8}{0.894}:\frac{0.894}{0.894}$

$=2.49:2.01:1$

This is approximately

$2.5:2:1$

Now multiply by $2$ to get whole numbers:

$5:4:2$

So the empirical formula is

$\mathrm{C}_{5}\mathrm{H}_{4}\mathrm{Br}_{2}$

From the empirical formula, number of carbon atoms $=5$.

$5$

text:
The pH of a solution obtained by mixing 5 mL of $0.1\mathrm{M}\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{OH}$ solution with 250 mL of $0.1\mathrm{M}\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{Cl}$ solution is $____$ $\times 10^{-2}$.(Nearest integer) Given: $\mathrm{pK}_{\mathrm{b}}(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{OH})=4.74$

$\begin{array}{l} \log 2=0.30 \\ \log 3=0.48 \\ \log 5=0.70 \end{array}$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For the mixture of a weak base and its salt, we use the buffer formula for a basic buffer:

$\mathrm{pOH}=\mathrm{p}K_{b}+\log \frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{base}]}$

Here,

Weak base $=\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{OH}$

Salt $=\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{Cl}$

Since both are mixed in the same final solution, we can use moles directly.

Step 1: Calculate moles of base
Volume of $\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{OH}=5\text{mL}=0.005\text{L}$

Molarity $=0.1\text{M}$

$n(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{OH})=0.1\times 0.005=5\times 10^{-4}\text{mol}$

Step 2: Calculate moles of salt
Volume of $\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{Cl}=250\text{mL}=0.250\text{L}$

Molarity $=0.1\text{M}$

$n(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{Cl})=0.1\times 0.250=2.5\times 10^{-2}\text{mol}$

Step 3: Apply buffer formula
$\mathrm{pOH}=4.74+\log \frac{2.5\times 10^{-2}}{5\times 10^{-4}}$

$\frac{2.5\times 10^{-2}}{5\times 10^{-4}}=50$

So,

$\mathrm{pOH}=4.74+\log 50$

Now,

$\log 50=\log (5\times 10)=\log 5+1=0.70+1=1.70$

Hence,

$\mathrm{pOH}=4.74+1.70=6.44$

Step 4: Find pH
$\mathrm{pH}=14-6.44=7.56$

Now write it in the form asked:

$7.56=756\times 10^{-2}$

Nearest integer $=756$

Final Answer:
$756$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift

text:
A non-volatile, non-electrolyte solid solute when dissolved in 40 g of a solvent, the vapour pressure of the solvent decreased from 760 mm Hg to 750 mm Hg . If the same solution boils at 320 K , then the number of moles of the solvent present in the solution is $____$ . (Nearest integer)

[Given: boiling point of the pure solvent $=319.5\mathrm{K}$,

$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{b}}$ of the solvent $=0.3\mathrm{K}\mathrm{kg}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ ]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute, first use relative lowering of vapour pressure:

$\frac{p^{0}-p}{p^{0}}=x_{2}$

where $x_{2}$ is the mole fraction of solute.

Given:

$p^{0}=760\text{mm Hg},p=750\text{mm Hg}$

So,

$x_{2}=\frac{760-750}{760}=\frac{10}{760}=\frac{1}{76}$

Now,

$x_{2}=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}+n_{2}}$

where $n_{1}$ = moles of solvent and $n_{2}$ = moles of solute.

Hence,

$\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}+n_{2}}=\frac{1}{76}$

This gives

$76n_{2}=n_{1}+n_{2}$

$n_{1}=75n_{2}$

Now use elevation in boiling point:

$\Delta T_{b}=K_{b}m$

Given:

$\Delta T_{b}=320-319.5=0.5\text{K}$

and

$K_{b}=0.3\text{K kg mol}^{-1}$

So molality,

$m=\frac{\Delta T_{b}}{K_{b}}=\frac{0.5}{0.3}=\frac{5}{3}$

But

$m=\frac{n_{2}}{\text{mass of solvent in kg}}$

Mass of solvent $=40\text{g}=0.040\text{kg}$

Thus,

$\frac{n_{2}}{0.040}=\frac{5}{3}$

$n_{2}=\frac{5}{3}\times 0.040=0.0667\text{mol}$

Now,

$n_{1}=75n_{2}=75\times 0.0667=5.00\text{mol}$

Therefore, the number of moles of solvent in the solution is

$5$

Nearest integer: $5$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift

text:
Amongst the following, the total number of compounds soluble in aqueous NaOH at room temperature is :

[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Aqueous NaOH dissolves a compound at room temperature only if it has an O–H acidic enough to be removed by $\mathrm{OH}{}^{-}$, i.e. a phenol ($\mathrm{p}K_{a}\approx 10$) or a carboxylic acid ($\mathrm{p}K_{a}\approx 4\text{–}5$); the sodium phenoxide or carboxylate formed is water-soluble.

Soluble: II (1-naphthol), III (4-(dimethylamino)phenol) and IV (p-cresol) are phenols; V (benzoic acid) and VII (1-naphthoic acid) are carboxylic acids.

Insoluble: I (benzaldehyde) has no acidic H, VI (N,N-dimethylcyclohexylamine) is a base, VIII (1,4-di-tert-butylbenzene) is a hydrocarbon, and IX (1-naphthylmethanol) is an alcohol ($\mathrm{p}K_{a}\approx 16$), not deprotonated by aqueous NaOH.

In IX the OH is on a $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}$ group attached to the ring, so unlike II it is not a phenol.

Number of compounds soluble in aqueous NaOH = 5.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

text:
Given below are two statements :
Statement I : The structure of Maltose is given below:

[IMG]

Statement II : The structure of Lactose is given below :

[IMG]

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 4th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Maltose and lactose are both disaccharides.

In each of these structures, one anomeric carbon is used to form the glycosidic linkage, but the other anomeric carbon remains free as a hemiacetal (–OH at anomeric carbon).

If a disaccharide has a free hemiacetal group, it can open up to the open-chain form and can reduce mild oxidising agents (like Tollens’ reagent or Fehling’s solution).

Therefore, both maltose and lactose are reducing sugars because both contain a hemiacetal linkage (free anomeric carbon).
